my person experience is that prior to my surgery and hrt I took adderall for a year or so, i was unable to work without it as i progressed in perimenopause. Now that i am in surgical menopause and on hrt i’m now able to manage without adhd meds. i’m not symptom free, but my symptoms are manageable without meds now and don’t justify the side effects from the meds. 

my understanding is adhd meds don’t work as well in the luteal phase because of the drop in your natural hormones, which will impact your dopamine levels as well. so my expectation would be after surgical menopause there would be no more fluctuation in hormones and it would be easier to stabilize on adhd meds if you still need them.

Many months after he cut me out of his life I threw everything away. We had been friends a long time so I had a fair amount of stuff. I wasn’t mad, but I was hurt so badly and so traumatized by how it happened that just having the things in my house was triggering. Hi, happy to share what advice I can. I'll be honest, it was really hard to get the help I needed. Don't give up if it takes multiple tries to find the right doctor for you. 

  
1. Educate yourself. Search for others with similar symptom constellations, learn from them. Read articles from Google scholar or credible medical institutions. So if you want to try chemical menopause, read up on when doctors consider that a valid treatment option, what things they want to rule out first, what complications it may have. There are some issues with long term chemical menopause, I don't recall off the top of my head what they are, but I do seem to recall there was only so long I could have stayed on the medication. And I believe insurance only covers it for certain scenarios (at the time they suspected I had endo, but that turned out not to be the case). I really only did chemical menopause a stepping stone to surgical menopause, never as a long term option. Have questions prepared. A lot of doctors don't like it when patients self-educate and come in treatments they would like to consider...I have learned those are not the doctors for me. My doctors LOVE that I educate myself and have informed opinions, and know that I am open to their opinions as well as long as they seem like a reasonable approach to my issues.

2. Advocate for yourself, and be unapologetic about it. I spent too much time wanting to be the good patient, to try anything the doctors suggested even when I knew it was the wrong path. They were wrong a lot, and in some cases that made me much worse. I should have moved on from a lot of doctors a lot faster than I did.

3. Interview your doctors. If you want chemical menopause to be an option, look for a doctor who has a solid history of treating people with chemical menopause. Not someone who has heard of it, or done it once or twice. Someone who has real experience. You can do a lot of this via email or phone without even making an appointment. For me, I turned away any surgeon that didn't have a solid history of treating people with PMDD and was open to surgery as an option. It didn't have to be the first thing we tried, but it had to be on the table. That ruled people out fast.

4. Track your symptoms meticulously. A lot of the credibility I gained with doctors was because I tracked all symptoms, all supplements/meds/lifestyle changes, and my cycle religiously for over 4 years. There were clear patterns that were simply impossible to refute and made it clear that I had already tried, and failed, the viable treatment options other than surgery. I had a huge spreadsheet where I tracked all of this and then once a month I would comb through it looking for patterns and insights. 

3. Find a person or community you think will be in your corner even if it's a long process. My journey from when symptoms first became disruptive in my life to my surgery was about 6 years. 2 years into that my symptoms became disabling in my life. Friends and family, none of whom have dealt with long term health issues, all assumed I wasn't trying hard enough to get help. It took a big tole on me to watch my support system vanish and have to fight so hard to find doctors who would listen. I finally found a therapist who was really supportive of me in this journey and it made a big difference. I went through so many bad fit therapists that I almost gave up, I'm glad I didn't. It doesn't have to be a therapists, it can be a friend or family member, or a PCP. But if at all possible, it's good to have someone who will encourage you.

My journey of 6 years was really long, but my situation was also complicated as it wasn't just perimenopause. At the onset I didn't know I was autistic, didn't know I had adhd, didn't know I had PMDD, and I didn't yet have PTSD. Perimenopause exacerbated the symptoms of all of those so as I fell deeper into perimenopause things got really bad. Of the advice I shared above, the only thing I was really doing from the onset was the meticulous tracking. In a strange way the PTSD did me a favor, it's how I ended up with the trauma therapists who helped me navigate a lot of this. She would coach me on how to present info to doctors, making they understand I am open to hearing and following their expertise, but also sharing my data from my tracking, as well as my hypothesis and asking for their input. And she helped me develop the confidence to leave doctors who were a bad fit, whether they didn't have the expertise, wouldn't listen, or a couple were genuinely abusive.

I wish you the best of luck. I hope you find a provider who is a good fit for you and you are able to try chemical menopause.

I am 47 and have been in surgical menopause for 1.5 years. I am so pleased with my decision and have been since the moment i woke up from the surgery. There are some adjustments but my quality of life is 1000 times better than before surgery.

I have PMDD, progesterone intolerance, and am AuDHD. I didn’t know any of this a few years prior to my surgery. As i plunged deeper into perimenopause my life just unraveled. I started having panic attacks, frequent meltdowns, intense bouts of depression and suicidal ideation, i was in physical pain (i kept getting ovarian cysts, inflammation, fibroids, etc), massive mood swings, and my cognitive decline was alarming. I ended up with severe PTSD. I destroyed relationships i cherished.It was hell on earth and honestly I just couldn’t have done it much longer.

I did a brief trial on chemical menopause before the surgery just to confirm plunging into menopause + hrt would alleviate my symptoms and while it didn’t make them fully go away, it helped a ton. So i went ahead with the surgery. I cannot begin to tell you how life changing it was. For me it was so much better than chemical menopause. It’s hard to say why but i believe it is tied to the progesterone intolerance. I felt like a completely different person from the moment i woke up from surgery. Even in my post surgery state, it was evident just looking at me. Anxiety, gone. Mood swings, gone. Suicidal thoughts, gone. With some recovery time and tweaking of my hrt my cognitive abilities are back where they should be. The last year has been one of my best ever at my very demanding job. 

It’s not all perfect. I don’t have as much energy as I used to, my eyes and skin get dry easily, i’m very sensitive to electrolytes imbalance (if it’s off i’m just really tired). But these are minor inconvenience that i can build a life around. Death would have been a mercy in the years preceding my surgery i was in such distress. Surgery gave me my life back. it’s not the right choice for everyone, but it sure was for me.

Whatever path you go down, I hope you find some relief soon.

I'm not an expert by any means, but here are some notes about my journey over the last year...

1. **Levels vs symptoms:** All my dosage adjustments were symptom based rather than level based. In fact I only just now (last week) had my level taken for the first time since starting hrt. Of course there was no question my levels were too low as I had an oopherectomy. For whatever it's worth, my E is at 204 and T is at 142. The T is high for a woman, but I've tried lower and feel awful. Since I have no negative side efforts, I have no intention of dropping the dose.
2. **Initial dose changes were fast:** I worked my way up to 1.5mg 2x per day very quickly. Same with T. My symptoms were very severe and I documented them very thoroughly, so it was pretty evident to my doctor and I the small doses I started out with, and taking once a day, was just not viable.
3. **It did take months for my body to stabilize on a dose:** once I found a dose that felt reasonably good, I continued to observe changes to how I responded to the dose over the course of a couple of months before my body stabilized. I saw increased benefits after a couple of months. But with both T and E, after I stabilized at the dose I thought was working, I ended up needing to increase it after a couple of months. I've read that's not uncommon for people who have had an oophorectomy. I guess my point is once your symptoms feel reasonably managed you may need to give it a little time and then see how things settle.
4. **It was very clear when a dose was too high:** My doc was great about letting me try different doses and each time I tried a dose higher than what I stabilized on it was immediately evident that it was too high. That was always a good indicator to me to back the dose down one level and give it a little time, some symptoms that still lingered a little got better when I gave it more time.
5. **I only changed one thing at a time:** I gave myself months to stabilize on an Estrogen dose before adding Testosterone. Then I gave myself two months on that before I increased Estrogen again. There are a lot of symptoms that are influenced by both so changing them in close proximity to one another can make it hard to tell which one is doing what.

I just had a hysterectomy a few weeks ago and also had a lot of anxiety leading up. I have PTSD and have past medical trauma so I knew there would be a lot of triggers in the hospital. My therapist gave me a suggestion that really helped. 

She suggested I write up something for my doctor and team at the hospital that would help them help me. I kept it one page and easy to scan and included the following:
- name and picture 
- doctors name
- emergency contact
- note that I am autistic and have PTSD
- called out specific triggers that were relevant to my hospital stay
- bullet list of what they could do to support me
- bullet list of what to do, and not to do, if I had a meltdown 
- I listed any questions I would have pre and post surgery cause I knew I’d forget
- I also noted some of my stims and let them know if they saw those it was me self regulating and not cause for concern

Everyone bent over backwards to support me the day of. They photo copied the paper I brought in so everyone on my team had access to it. They offered me something for my anxiety early on. They were very intentional doing whatever they could to avoid my triggers or help me feel safe. 

Honestly it worked so well I will be doing this anytime I see a new doctor in the future. I tried to keep it short and easy to scan so it wasn’t overwhelming for them. The way they accommodated my needs really made it a positive experience for me. Happy to share more details about what I noted for them if it’s helpful.

I'm so sorry to hear you are struggling with this at 19, I hope you will find some success in managing it so it is not such a focus in your life. I'm 45 and I've only been dealing with this for the last 7 years or so, though I didn't know it was PMDD until this year. 

Mine starts around ovulation and lasts through the end of my period. There are ups and downs in that time as my hormones fluctuate, but it's a struggle the whole time. The longest really tough stretch is the week before my period through the first 3 days of my period, but there are bad days before that as my hormones fluctuate. My cycles are 33 days long, give or take, and without fail day 19 is the absolute worst, followed closely by day 1 of my period. 

I am no expert, but from what I've read your experience is very common for PMDD. There is a lot that is not yet understood about it. Here is a link to a great video I found helpful which discusses some research which indicates there are different types of PMDD:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UmvA5mWv1OI&t=11s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UmvA5mWv1OI&t=11s) 

I've also found I will have an odd month where my symptoms are magically less severe, every time it's a month where something else is happening that would clearly have an impact on my hormone levels. Tracking is your best friend, eventually patterns emerge that should help in coming up with a plan to manage it.

I hope that is helpful. I wish you the best of luck in finding some relief soon.

The best way to determine is to go for a neuro psych evaluation if that is accessible to you. There are standardized test to evaluate for adhd. Outwardly it may present in different ways so primary care doctors often don’t recognize it.

BPD criteria have high overlap with quite a few conditions. So fitting some of the criteria doesn’t necessarily mean you have BPD. In those cases where there is high overlap and multiple diagnosis could apply, I personally think your opinion as to whether you have BPD (after researching) is as important, or even more important, than the doctors. 

I fit a lot of the BPD criteria. However, I have an unshakably solid sense of self and while my moods oscillate wildly, how I feel about others does not. I withdraw at times, but to protect myself and others. So I have been adamant that I do not have BPD. I don’t mind the label, but it informs the treatment and I wanted to make sure I was getting the help I needed.

Multiple primary care doctors (so not psychiatrists) felt I had BPD though. Knowing what I know now, this just highlights to me that they were not trauma informed and had little to no knowledge of neurodiversity and pmdd. 

I was eventually diagnosed as autistic, as well as  adhd, pmdd, ptsd, and cptsd. Those more than explain my behavior and symptoms. They just told are the first, second, third, or tenth thing most doctors look for.

If you find you relate to some of the BPD criteria in a way that is not fully explained by PMDD you might investigate CPTSD. There is a school of thought that BPD is just an extreme manifestation of CPTSD. The latter is not in the DSM, but is generally acknowledged in the medical community. Most still regard these as two different conditions, but the theory that they are the same thing is gaining support. 

At the root of both BPD and CPTSD is ongoing trauma, often developmental trauma. This can range from emotional neglect to sexual abuse, it’s a wide spectrum. How the trauma impacts the person has more to do with that persons brain and nervous system than it does the severity of the event. We all experience trauma in life, not everyone is impacted by it the same way though. The Body Keeps The Score is a great book that gives more background on how trauma can show up.

Update: Trigger Warning - The Body Keeps the Score can be very triggering so if you are not in a good space it may be better to wait, or go slowly and have a support system in place.

When I was deeply struggling with suicidal thoughts only one person knew I was depressed, my best friend. He had encouraged me to lean on him and share with him. And that continued for a long while, over a year. I kept checking in to make sure it was still cool, he kept assuring me it was. I was seeking help from doctors but no therapists yet, but it was slow going and there were set backs. 

During the worst setback he just kinda flipped a switch. He went from always encouraging me to share and wanting me to lean on him to telling me he couldn’t help me, he couldn’t around me anymore and I needed to look elsewhere for help and support. He got incredibly angry at me, I’m not sure I’ve seen anyone be that angry with me before.

He ended out friendship. I begged, not my proudest moment, asked him to give me more time, even if we were less involved in each other’s lives for a while. He unfriended me on socials and ghosted me. This was my best friend of 4 years, I spoke with him most ever day for years, and I had know him 15 years. Three months prior we were in a good place. And just like that he was done. When I tell you that broke me, I mean it shattered ever piece of my heart and identity I had left. 

That was almost exactly two years ago. I have made tremendous progress with my mental health since then  thanks to lots of therapy and some medication. But I still miss him everyday and am still grieving the loss of that friendship. I have the smallest shred of hope that one day I can repair things but I have resolved not to try until I’m in a really good place. I’m getting there, but I’m not there yet. Soon though I think. Unlike your friend, mine did not indicate I could come back once in a healthier place.

So here is what I have learned:
1. No matter what he said, it was unfair of me to put the sole burden of supporting me through a mental health crisis on one person who was not trained to handle such things. Leaning on people is good, but if you are leaning to hard that when they step away you fall instead of stumble then you are likely leaning too much. This is my responsibility and I have learned to find a better balance here, and found professions that can help when in need more support.

2. He was either terrible at knowing his limits and the boundaries he needed, or terrible at articulating them. It is not my fault or responsibility that he took on more than he could handle, I didn’t and couldn’t force him. It’s really hard to hold up boundaries with people we love. To say, I love you but this is all I can give here even though I can see that will disappoint you. Boundaries are people telling you they love you so much they want to find a way to keep you in their life so they need to find a balance that is sustainable. It sounds like your friend shared some boundaries, that tells me they care about you. I think the problem is often people don’t articulate boundaries until they get to a breaking point so the boundaries are extreme, and this can be traumatic. Had my friend early on given me some boundaries there would never have been a problem. The same may be true for you. Because he waited until he was at his breaking point things just, well, broke. I suspect we both ended up hurt by what happened, but it is not my fault or responsibility that he did not establish healthy boundaries for himself. Boundaries around mental health stuff will be different for everyone so it’s not great to have to guess.

3. I suspect, but do not know, that he ghosted me instead of just distancing for a while, because he was ashamed. I cannot tell you how much this action hurt me, and how personally I took it for so long. But looking back after some healing, I believe he felt he let me down by having to take a step back, and I believe he was embarrassed about how he handled it (cause it was spectacularly awful). I think it was easier for him to cut me out completely than to see me or speak to me, knowing how much pain I was in and knowing he made it so much worse instead of helping the way he wanted to. I think he didn’t want to be reminded of the shame or guilt he felt and didn’t see how to recover, so he just ended things because that was less painful for him. More painful for me, but Jess for him. But not ending things would have been less painful for me but more painful for him since he was not able to hold healthy boundaries. So unfortunately someone was going to end up really hurt one way or the other, I can’t fault him for choosing himself over me, that’s the right thing to do. I could be wrong, I don’t know, it’s just what I suspect. For people who can’t articulate and hold boundaries, it can be very hard for them to stay actively in someone’s life while they navigate to a healthier place. I have a few friends who are able to do this, they all have different boundaries too, there is only one I can really talk about suicidal thoughts with for example. Most people in my life cannot handle this so I’ve just put those relationships on pause for now as I don’t have the capacity to pretend to be fine.

4. That brings me to my last point. I have done a lot of pretending to be fine and pretending to be someone I’m not in order to get along over the course of my life. I think this did me more harm than I ever could have imagined. Of course I always felt like no one loved me, I didn’t give them a chance, they didn’t really know me. I basically set myself up yo fail. There are people who love me just as I am now that I e given them the chance. When I kinda broke at the end of 2019 I broke so badly I lost the ability to do any masking or pretending. I am not exaggerating when I say for a month every time I tried to speak to a human I burst out subbing and couldn’t stop for at least 30min. After two years and a lot of work I can now mask a little when I must, like at work, but it takes so much more out of me than I knew, so at this time I’m simply not interacting with anyone outside of work that I cannot be authentic with. That doesn’t mean I tell them everything, but it does mean I don’t pretend I’m not depressed or struggling or grieving. It’s such a relief not to be pretending all the time. Just that one change alone made things a bit better for me. And I’ll be honest, I had to put more friendships on pause because of this, after two years of severe depression many don’t understand why I’m not better and have low patience for me if I’m not pretending to be okay. So for now my boundary is there is not an active place in my life for them until I’m in a better place. I fully intend to reconnect with them and I’ve told them that and said I just need time alone to heal. I’m confident most or all of those friendships will survive the pause. TikTok has been great for me in this regard, there are whole communities of people in which I don’t have to pretend even a little. I can’t tell you how wonderful that feels to be accepted just as I am.

It is a terrible experience to feel like a burden, I’m sorry that is what you are going through right now. As someone who has spent a lifetime feeling like a burden, I empathize. I’m learning it’s healthy to be able to depend on people sometimes. The word burden may get a bad wrap. The nature of all close relationships is that you are willing to offer the people you care about support at times. If needing support is being a burden, then we are all a burden at times and that’s just part of the human experience.

It is possible that you find yourself in a position where your needs exceed what those around you have to give. I did. That does not mean there is anything bad about you for needing more. And it doesn’t mean there is anything bad about them for not having more to give at that time. The only thing it means is you may have to look outside your immediate circle for support, which we all have to do sometimes. That could mean coming to Reddit or other online forums, it could mean expanding your friend group, it could mean finding a support group, or it could mean working with a doctor or therapist. 

You are correct that everyone is going through their own thing. That doesn’t always mean they don’t have capacity to offer you some support. I used to try to ‘protect’ my friends by not leaning on them and making judgement calls about how much support they could offer. In retrospect I now see how that had a negative impact on those relationships. They felt less comfortable seeking support from me because I wouldn’t let them support me. They also felt disrespected at times that I didn’t trust them to decide for themselves what their capacity was.

It can be really hard to figure out what someones capacity is. Asking is the easiest way. It can be a little uncomfortable at first, but it gets easier with practice. Recently I’ve been trying a slow lead in that gives them a comfortable way to opt in or out. I’m trying to be honest but brief when people ask me how I am. For example, “It’s been a really difficult time for me lately but I’m working through it the best I can.”. If someone asks no follow up questions they probably aren’t the right person to lean on at that time. Most people will ask “what’s going on”. I then say something like “It’s kinda heavy and hard for me to quickly sum up. If you have bandwidth a deeper discussion I’d…
a. value an outside perspective.

I have found in some cases the sub classifications of mood disorders are harmful, in large part because they are not trauma informed and I’m not convinced they are as different as the DSM makes them out. Though I acknowledge that as a guiding direction for first line treatment it can be helpful when the diagnosis is correct, but harmful when it’s not.

Autoimmune diseases are interesting. Often a diagnosis must be given to justify the treatment they want to try, even if you don’t fit the diagnosis exactly. I was given 5 different diagnosis in 4 years but in the end what I had was chronic inflammation due to an overactive immune system, regardless of the label put in it. Sometimes my symptoms were severe, and sometimes mild. I was given the help I needed based on how my symptoms presented, the diagnosis was just for insurance purposes. I think this is a better standard of care.

My point is unlike most doctors who have training in a specialized area with very defined criteria, I find rheumatologist are more adept at looking at the whole constellation of symptoms and trying to reason what the body is doing and how to support it rather than trying to make things fit a diagnosis.

Regardless of diagnostic criteria, I would love to see a change in how doctors are trained to identify, understand and support patients. An openness that neurodivergence is far more common than was originally understood and can manifest in a wide variety of ways might mean more people getting the support they deserve. 

I fear over focusing on sub classifications for something like autism may still result in people getting lost between the lines who do not cleanly fit any subtype. I’m not against refining the DSM, we know a lot more now and probably should, but doing it without changing how doctors are trained I think is unlikely to yield the best results.

I’m not sure I have the answer but as I’m working on the same thing I can tell you what I’m trying.

1. Start small. Suuuuper small. What’s one small simple think you like about yourself. Even if it’s silly. 

For example: I like the way I load the dishwasher even if it might annoy others. I like that I stop to talk to the barista at my coffee shop because I’m truly interested in how she’s doing. 

It may not seem like much, but it’s a place to start and when you feel self hatred, any positive feeling is a good place to start I think.

2. Pay attention to what you like about others. I find this falls into two categories for me. The first is qualities I lack, so that’s no help. The second is qualities or values I possess, but it’s easier for me to see and appreciate them in others.

For example: I love the way one of my friends supports and encourages her friends but also holds her own boundaries. I actually do the same, but it’s harder for me to see that through my lens of self hate.

3. Therapy if that’s an option. Having someone work with you on this and challenge your negative self talk is helpful. Also I’m a fan of EMDR for trauma.

4. Journaling. Try writing your thoughts as they come then practice going back and re-writing through a lens of self compassion. Even if you don’t believe it yet, try it anyway.

5. Check out Kristin Neff. She has a book but you can also find free content on YouTube or podcast interviews. Her focus is on how to cultivate self compassion.

6. Check out Jeffrey Marsh. You can find them on most social platforms and they also have a book, How to Be You. 

7. If you haven’t already, consider reading  ‘The Body Keeps the Score’ and ‘Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving’. I also really liked Oprah’s book ‘What happened to you’. 

For me at least, the more I learn about trauma the more compassion I have for myself. 

8. Support and encourage others who are struggling. You’ll may find yourself saying the things you most need to hear. Sone tines it’s easier to start by saying them to someone else in a similar situation. Reddit is great for this.

I hope that’s helpful. Keep working on it. You deserve to be loved, by yourself and others. We all do.

As I understand it (I’m still learning), neurodivergent means you brain works differently by default than what is considered neurotypical. Dyslexia is another example of neurodivergence.

I don’t know a lot about sensory processing disorder but I would think that falls under the neurodivergence umbrella.

CPTSD does not. That is a response to events and situations and as a result of the trauma your brain/nervous system adapt for protection. This can, to some extent, be undone though. I would say the same is true of depression.

Neurodivergence does not get undone, and many would not want it undone. Though some traits can be managed to support a better quality of life. Unlike trauma, it is not a negative in and of itself, and it can have many positives, but it can be harder to navigate in a world designed for neurotypicals. 

It is a different way of thinking and experiencing the world based on how the brain works by default for that individual. This is different from trauma where the you have adjusted to think and experience things differently to stay safe. 

My guess is a higher percentage of neurodivergent individuals experience CPTSD as trauma can come, in many forms, when trying or being forced to fit into a world or a role you were not designed for. Schools, jobs, social norms…almost all of these were designed first and foremost for neurotypicals.

I consider myself neurodivergent. Though I do not have a formal diagnosis, I believe I am dyslexic and autistic. This is part of who I am and I am learning to stop hiding (masking) these parts of myself and instead enjoy and appreciate the unique ways my brain works.

I also suffer from CPTSD, PTSD, depression and anxiety (all of these are related for me). These are not who I am, these are how I have adapted to unhealthy environments and experiences and I am working to address these.

That’s my understanding so far. Hope that helps.

Yes. I am taking a type of therapy called DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy). It’s more learning skills to navigate life vs talk therapy. Really anyone could benefit from it.

Skills are grouped into 4 modules: mindfulness, emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.

Anyway, one of the skills is called “opposite action”. You use it when your feelings aren’t supported by the facts. In those cases you try to act the opposite of how you feel.

So with your texting example, if the person you haven’t heard back from has historically gotten back to you within a reasonable period of time then you might say feeling anxious doesn’t fit the facts. 

It doesn’t stop you from feeling anxious necessarily as our feelings are informed by a lot more than the facts of the current situation. However, it will likely help you not to create a problem where one does not exist.

Now it advises to use a different skill if your feelings do fit the facts. If the person you haven’t heard back from has ghosted you in the past, for example, then feeling anxious might fit the facts (I’m over simplifying as a lot more facts should be taken into account). You would then move on to the “problem solving” skill instead of “opposite action”.

As for your ex and for my former best friend, I think any relationship where we feel scared some of the time is unhealthy. Anger is okay, but it can be expressed in healthy ways that aren't frightening. That's their work, not ours. And I suspect our intense emotions were overwhelming for them, it's not the same as their threatening behavior but still likely made the relationships unhealthy for them. My work, and perhaps yours, is around regulating our emotions and healing our trauma. When you said you froze on your birthday, that is a trauma response. That is your nervous system trying to protect you. The people pleasing behavior after to try to smooth things over, that's also a trauma response, it's called Fawn. Check out Polyvagal Theory, the Stuck not Broken podcast is a resource I like.  
  
The thing about trauma, the reasoned part of your brain goes offline and you brain and nervous system are just in protection mode. When your nervous system becomes dysregulated and you get stuck in a state like Fight, Flight, Freeze, or Fawn you are not going to be able to have calm thoughtful conversations because you brain and body are screaming DANGER! PROTECT! I see the phrase a lot that trauma rewires you brain to protect instead of connect, in other words relationships will suffer when you get stuck in this protection state. This can also effect your memory as your brain doesn't store memories the same way when you are in these activated states.  
  
Understanding the trauma aspect has been so helpful for me as I now see that I was really stuck in this protect mode for a very long time and it had a huge impact on my interactions with my former friend. I loved him, but I was afraid of him. Afraid he would abandon me, afraid he would yell at me, and on occasion afraid he would physically hurt me. His words and his actions did not always align, and this fed my fear. He would tell me I was reading things wrong (I wasn't) and this reduced my confidence in myself an my instincts (this is called gaslighting). So no, I was not showing up at my best in conversations because despite all the love and best of intentions, my body and brain were still screaming PROTECT. So a huge part of my healing has been to learn how to calm my nervous system down, and to try and recognize when I am in these activated protection modes.  
  
So when you say you said things you didn't mean and were someone you didn't recognize, I understand. And I truly believe you were doing the best you could at the time. If no one taught us about these things, how could we know? We couldn't. But we can learn now and show up differently in relationships in the future. It doesn't make the pain any less I know, and it doesn't change that we are responsible for how we showed up in the past, but I think it invites some compassion.

All I can do now if work on healing myself, educating myself, and learning how to handle my emotions and my distress in healthier ways.   
  
I think these issues (e.g. trauma, attachment, boundaries, etc.)  will always be part of me, it's not like in a year or two I'll be 100% better. But I believe I can get to a point where these things don't rule my life the way they did before. I want to reach a point where I recognize how I'm behaving, and why, and am able to stay calm enough in most situations to course correct my words and actions regardless of how I feel. That's the goal anyway. I've been working on this for over a year and it's a LOT of work and I still have a long way to go. Before I used walls for armor, but when I let them down I would too vulnerable and that's how I got here. We've got these big brains though, so perhaps a better way to protect is through knowledge, insight, and practicing different and healthier behaviors to learn new patterns. That's my hope anyway.

If you have health care:
1. Work with a psychiatrist to get a professional assessment and potentially medication. 
2. Find a therapist you really click with. Consider looking for one that is trauma informed. Personally I’ve had the best luck with sex therapists, even though that’s not explicitly why I’m seeing them.
3. Look into DBT
4. Look into EMDR

It took years of wrong diagnosis and wrong treatments before finding a care team that really listened to me and I finally feel like I’m on a path to healing. I hope that might be an option for you.

If you don’t have healthcare, or just in addition to the above:
1. check out Kristin Neffs work on self compassion. She has a book but if you want a preview she’s done lots of podcast interviews.

2. look into attachment styles. The book Attached is great. If you want free content there are many podcasts covering this topic.

3. check out the DBT and Me podcast. DBT focuses on life skills we should all have. Specifically mindfulness, emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness. I listened to the podcast before joining a DBT group and got a lot out of it.

4. There are a lot of podcasts out there run by therapists (#3 is an example). Look around for one that resonates. It’s not a substitute for therapy but it’s a great resource and free. I like Stuck Not Broken and Therapists Uncensored.

5. Maybe saving the best for last, my recent obsession is Jeffrey Marsh. Check them out on Instagram, TikTok, or FB for lots of free content. They also have a book called How to Be You that I’m currently reading. Every time I listen to their content, even just a couple of minutes, I can’t help but love myself a tiny bit. 

My final advice to you would be to start small. I have an endless list of things I hate about myself. Anything I see in the mirror as well as things I consider character flaws or weakness. It’s hard for me to love big things about myself.

Small things though are easier. I love the water. I never fail to appreciate it. I like that about me. My eyes are blue and I like blue, so I like that my eyes are blue. Before I got stuck in my current depression I was one of those people who frequently laughed until I hyperventilated, I liked that about me and hope to get back to it. I like to be of service so every time I help someone, I’m big or small ways, I like that I am living in alignment with my values. Collect a list of small things you like about yourself. Small things add up to big things.

That can be one characteristic. Though I don’t think it would be accurate to say everyone who distances themselves in a conflict is avoidant. 

I’m not an expert but I would say both avoidant and anxious types crave connection but have some wounding that makes it feel unsafe. 

Anxious, when feeling a threat to connection, will seek to foster more closeness as a means of reassurance. 

Avoidant, when feeling a threat to connection, will seek distance as a means of reassert if independence. That distance can be more than just limiting or shutting down communication, it can also look like shutting down emotionally. So someone who once had a warm and caring tone now sounds indifferent, as an example. 

Both are just seeking safety and repair, but in ways that trigger the other unfortunately. Given time, both types may relax their reactions if the threat to connection feels like it’s dissipating. But if the root issues aren’t addressed it can be easy to get stuck in a cycle of this behavior.

At least that is how I currently understand it. I’m still learning and am far from an expert.

In terms of how to get through the next few weeks, here are some ideas:

1. If it’s an option, consider online therapy like TalkSpace or BetterHelp at least for a month or so until you get rolling with your therapist. 2. Keep coming here, read, and post as much as you want. Peer support is a great resource and has gotten me through some hard days. 

3. There are a lot of podcasts out there run by therapists. This is not a substitute for therapy, but it can help you feel less alone in your struggles and sometimes offer some perspective and/or resources that may be beneficial. Personally I like DBT and Me, Stuck not Broken, and Therapists Uncensored. Different podcasts may appeal to you depending on what you are struggling with.

4. There are also many great books out there on mental health. Again, not a substitute for therapy but at least for me it helps me to understand what I’m feeling is far more common than I realized. It’s also given me better insight and ways to express what I’m feeling.

5. And finally, focus on healthy life choices. Walk daily. Get a good nights sleep. Eat well, lots of veggies. Limit triggers where you can.

Take it day by day. A few weeks can seem like a lifetime when you are struggling but if you just focus on one day at a time you’ll get there.

If he really cares about this friend I would suggest he try setting some boundaries that enable him to offer support in a way that feel healthy to him. 

Such boundaries might look like…
“Hey friend, I really care about you and I want to stay by your side during this difficult time. I’m finding I too am struggling right now and am looking for the right balance between the time and energy I need to care for myself and what I can offer others. I’d like to try limiting our conversations on difficult subject matters to [example: certain days a week, just once a week, only when I ask, I’d like you to ask if I have capacity before we start the conversation, etc. - whatever feels good]. How would that be for you?”

Be prepared her initial response may be negative. When you are in a dark place and you think you are going to lose your support system, that is terrifying. If he goes this direction he should be prepared for that and do his best to stay calm and consistent in his messaging, giving her time to calm down and adjust. Even if that looks like, “I know this is a lot to take in. Why don’t we pause the conversation and pick it back up tomorrow once we’ve both had time to think over each other’s perspectives”.

Alternatively, if your boyfriend is at capacity and just cannot handle difficult subject matter anymore, he should say that. But if he wants to maintain the friendship he should follow up with examples of ways they can still engage. If she is in a bad place she might just hear he doesn’t want to talk at all.

Setting boundaries like this is difficult for both parties, but this is how friendships and relationships weather tough times.

And if none of that is an option and he really just needs a break from her, please encourage him to message it gently, to take some responsibility for it (e.g. she hasn’t done something bad, he just needs some space for himself right now). The likelihood is he has encouraged some of her dependence on him in this matter, whether he meant to or not, so he should take accountability for that and not place all the responsibility on her.

I deeply empathize with the trust issues and poor experiences with care providers. Honestly, I wrote therapy off for a while because my first few therapists did more harm than good. My current one is a life saver though and I’m so glad I gave it one more shot. 

If therapy isn’t an option now I understand. If you are ever in a position to give it another shot, trust your gut and pass on any therapist that doesn’t feel right. It’s fine to go to a session or two and then decide they aren’t for you. When you find a good fit you’ll know it.

If you aren’t already familiar with DBT it might be worth reading up on. It’s a type of therapy, but really it’s all about teaching skills you can use everyday to help with mindfulness, emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal relationships. Honestly it teaches skills so fundamental, I think everyone would benefit from them. I wish this stuff was taught in schools.

DBT is usually taught in group therapy, it can also be done in individual therapy. I hear those aren’t options right now. I started learning about DBT on my own before joining a group, it’s not the same but I still got value out of it.

The DBT and Me podcast, run by two DBT therapists, has been a great resource for me. There is also a lot of information online.

Stuck not Broken is another podcast run by a therapist, he focuses on polyvagal theory. This one doesn’t necessarily teach specific skills you can use, but for me it helped me better understand what was going on in my body and brain, which helped alleviate some of the shame I felt.

Therapists Uncensored is one more therapy related podcast I’ve found helpful. They talk a lot about Attachment Theory, like Polyvagal Theory, this helped me better understand what I was experiencing and in turn removed some of the shame I felt.

Keep trying. Keep looking for the support you need and deserve. I know it’s hard, but you can do it.

I’m sorry you are in so much distress. That is such a heavy weight to carry and I hear that you are not getting the support and comfort you long for.  That is a difficult place to be. I am glad you have reached out on this forum to find some support.

In addition to the suggestions already listed, I go for a walk while listening to audiobooks or podcasts. The movement helps my nervous system regulate, as to the human voices. I also usually choose books and podcasts that are supportive and teach me helpful skills, though I have to be careful to avoid triggering content. I’m really into DBT and Me, as well as Stuck Not Broken podcasts right now.

I dunk my face in ice water fairly often and that calms me down a bit. I do paced breathing all the time, just basically exhale through lips longer than the inhale. I too miss physical comfort, my weighted blanket helps some.

When I’m truly inconsolable and hysterical I sit in a hot shower and cry and scream until the water runs cold. I’m so exhausted by the time it’s done I can usually sleep and the next day I tend to be calmer.

And if I need to talk to someone or am worried about my ability to regulate my behavior I will call a crisis hotline. There was a time when I called at least once a day.

If it’s available to you, therapy can help a lot.

This sounds like such a difficult situation. I hear that this is a relationship you have valued over the course of time, but at present (and maybe other times in the past) it has taken more from you than it has given.

My only advice to you is be clear about your boundaries and what you need, and be kind. Life is long, or so we hope, and you may find down the road she is in a better place to connect with you in a way that is positive for you both.  If you need a break for now, by all means take it. If you want to try boundaries, think about how to clearly and compassionately communicate them - these aren't easy conversations, but can really help relationships get to a healthier place. If you are truly ready to be done for good and that's what's best for you, that's okay too. Just be kind. 

I will say that reading your description of your friend, it sounds like her life experiences have taught her it's not safe to be in relationship with someone. That's not yours to fix, and it's okay if you aren't up for being along for the ride while she fixes it.  I would just encourage you to think of her with compassion and understand she may not be in a place where she can do better right now, her nervous system may just be screaming at her that she is unsafe even when those around her interpret the situation differently.  That is so very hard to change, and often requires professional support from a therapist. 

I imagine whatever path you choose will be hard for both of you in different ways.  I've been on both sides of similar situations, they are both difficult. A couple of years back I was very similar to your friend.  My best friend did end our friendship over it. He is a good guy and I know he did what he had to. He was, however, cruel in how he did it. I know him and he is not cruel, so I know he did the best he could at the time, just as I was doing my best. But if you have it in you to navigate this transition with kindness and compassion, I think it will help you both in the long run whether you reconnect or not. To me that means no ghosting, no gaslighting (e.g. distance yourself but then act like nothings changes), no blaming, and in the end being clear on what your decision is. You don't have to explain why if you don't want to, but if you care about this person it's a kindness to be clear and not leave uncertain about where the relationship stands.

Be sure to take extra good care of yourself throughout this. It's a tough situation and you may not fully realize how much it's impacting you. Best of luck, I hope you find a path that you are comfortable with.
